practicalQuestion: When symptoms and clinic-based measures have normalized but high-speed and sport-specific exposure remain incomplete, how should physical therapy and performance staff structure the next 7–10 days and define progress, hold, or regress criteria without relying on a single return-to-sport cutoff?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athlete nearing unrestricted participation after a lower-extremity injury
decisionContext.sport: Field sport with sprinting, cutting, and reactive demands
decisionContext.phase: Modified participation to unrestricted team activity
decisionContext.outcome: Coordinate staged exposure and decision ownership across rehabilitation and performance staff
decisionContext.constraints: Limited practice opportunities; competition schedule continues; no athlete-identifying or diagnosis-specific data

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source in the pack tests a 7 to 10 day late-stage structure or validated progress, hold or regress criteria. The most direct evidence is one ACL reconstruction case series and one single-player ACL case study, both in male soccer. The case study describes strength benchmarks used to gate running speed. One digest summary of a collegiate study found that hamstring strength and asymmetry at return to sport did not differ between athletes who did and did not re-injure. Sprint-exposure findings come from observational data in healthy professional or elite soccer squads, with hamstring injury or strength outcomes. Sources disagree on whether asymmetry should guide progression, so the brief sets out options rather than a recommended direction.

dimensions.sourceReview: All cited claims are checked against original source text. The designs are a case series, a single case study, a retrospective observational analysis, an observational cohort, an observational team study, a practitioner survey, and digest summaries of a collegiate cross-sectional study, a meta-analysis, a narrative review and editorials.
dimensions.directness: The evidence is partly direct on the gap between late on-field rehabilitation loads and published team training and match demands, and on criteria practitioners report using. It is indirect on near-maximal speed dosing and timing, which come from healthy squads rather than rehabilitating athletes. No source tests decision criteria for a 7 to 10 day window.
dimensions.consistency: The sources agree that controlled rehabilitation work falls short of match demands. They conflict on the role of limb asymmetry. Near-maximal speed exposure two days before a match was linked to zero match hamstring injuries in one dataset, but pooled exposure showed no difference in injury rate. In another cohort, 7 to 8 weekly efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were linked to very small eccentric strength decreases.
dimensions.transferability: Most participants were male soccer players, either after ACL reconstruction or in healthy professional and elite squads. One digest summary covers collegiate Division I athletes after hamstring strain. The ACL case series authors state their findings are most likely not applicable to female players. No source studied this exact late-stage setting in collegiate field-sport athletes.

bottomLine.text: Normal symptoms and clinic measures do not close the gap to match demands. In male soccer players after ACL reconstruction, final-stage field rehabilitation came close to published team training loads, but deceleration lagged and every metric stayed below match play. Near-maximal speed exposure and its timing relative to a match may matter, but the data come from healthy squads and are observational. In collegiate athletes after hamstring strain, strength and asymmetry at return to sport did not separate those who re-injured. No source validates a single cutoff or tests a progress, hold or regress framework, so staff will need agreed multi-marker criteria built partly from professional judgment.

actions.title: Option: close the measured gap to match demands in controlled field sessions
actions.text: In the ACL reconstruction case series, final-stage loads matched or exceeded published team training values for high-intensity distance and accelerations. Peak speed reached 88% and deceleration distance 48% of team training, and all metrics were below match play. Only 33 of 100 players reached the final stage, which lasted a mean of about 10 days with wide variation. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): one option is to use the early days of the window for targeted peak speed and deceleration exposure, with each day's targets set against the athlete's own team and match references rather than total distance.

actions.title: Option: use partial team sessions for reactive, high neuromuscular demands
actions.text: The ACL case series authors state that field rehabilitation did not fully prepare players for full team training and point to further training, such as modified training, before full integration. In a single-player case study, the late return phases were about load management, including partial team sessions where the player took part in only some drills or played small-sided games as a floater. The same authors state that high-intensity work with large neuromuscular demands is required toward the end of the return process. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): limit the first team exposures to defined drills and durations agreed in advance by physical therapy and performance staff.

actions.title: Option: schedule near-maximal speed exposure relative to the next competition
actions.text: In retrospective data from healthy players in elite soccer squads, there were no match hamstring injuries when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed occurred two days before a match. This is an association; pooled across all turnarounds, exposure showed no difference in injury rate. The authors suggest the two-days-before timing may apply to the whole squad for 6 to 8 day turnarounds but may only concern substitutes for 3 to 5 day turnarounds. In the single-player ACL case, the authors used strength benchmarks before allowing speeds close to maximum. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with a roughly weekly schedule, staff could plan one near-maximal exposure about two days before the next fixture once strength benchmarks are met, and keep the day before it lighter.

actions.title: Option: agree on multi-marker progress, hold and regress rules in advance
actions.text: Brazilian elite club physical therapists reported progressing hamstring rehabilitation mostly on pain, strength and functional status, and used strength and sprint or high-speed running as the only return criteria applied by more than half of respondents. A load management editorial states that training loads may need to be sensibly regressed to limit fatigue, pain, performance reductions and reinjury risk, without prolonged reductions. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): one approach is to progress when planned speed and deceleration exposures are completed without symptom recurrence or strength decline, hold when a marker stalls, and regress when symptoms or strength worsen. Name in writing who owns each call.

actions.title: Option: add top-up exposure when practice or match time is limited
actions.text: In one professional reserve squad, players with more match time accumulated more weekly load, particularly total distance and high metabolic load distance. The authors interpret that the compensatory session for players with limited match time did not seem to provide enough high-speed running and sprint overload. With limited practice opportunities, staff could add supplementary high-speed field exposure. These data come from healthy players, and the evidence does not test whether top-ups improve return outcomes.

monitoring.label: Exposure against team and match references
monitoring.text: Track high-intensity distance, peak speed, accelerations and decelerations against team training and match references. The case series compared against published values because preinjury GPS data were lacking. Total distance plateaued across stages, and the authors judged it not useful for return decisions or stage progression.

monitoring.label: Deceleration
monitoring.text: Deceleration distance was the furthest behind team training at the final rehabilitation stage, at 48%. The case series authors suggest lower deceleration workloads could affect return and reinjury risk but call for research on that impact. An editorial commentary describes deceleration as a key, often overlooked rehabilitation component.

monitoring.label: Near-maximal efforts and eccentric hamstring strength
monitoring.text: In professional male soccer players, weekly efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were the only sprint measure that significantly influenced weekly eccentric hamstring force change. The differences were about a tenth of a percent, and the study did not measure injury. Efforts above 95% were too rare to assess. The authors suggest monitoring weekly efforts above 90% may be valuable. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): pair the count with a regular eccentric strength check.

monitoring.label: Asymmetry, interpreted cautiously
monitoring.text: One case study proposes step impulse asymmetry to guide phase progression; in that case, asymmetry and pain resolved together on a softer pitch. In collegiate athletes after hamstring strain, eccentric strength asymmetry at return to sport did not differ between those who did and did not re-injure. A narrative review found no evidence that pre-existing asymmetries increase injury risk. Use asymmetry as context, not as a stand-alone gate.

guardrails.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): this brief informs criteria and monitoring only. Progression and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians. Practitioners reported heterogeneous criteria, and no source validates one decision rule.

The two-days-before-match finding is a retrospective association with match hamstring injuries in healthy elite squads, the pooled comparison showed no difference, and the authors limit the timing to substitutes for short turnarounds. The Gaelic exposure values are cited background that the authors note is relative to Gaelic football demands. Do not treat either as a prescribed dose or timing rule.

Competition is a higher-risk setting than training. Across field-based team sports, hamstring injury incidence was 9.4-fold higher in matches. Even full rehabilitation stages left loads below match play. Plan the first competitive minutes as a separate step.

Do not let any single metric, such as total distance, a strength value or a limb asymmetry value, act as the return cutoff. Total distance was judged not useful, strength and asymmetry at return did not separate re-injured collegiate athletes, and asymmetry is contested.

limitations.text: Populations were male soccer players after ACL reconstruction (an amateur and professional case series and one professional player), healthy professional and elite soccer squads, a Spanish reserve squad, Brazilian elite men's club physical therapists, and collegiate Division I athletes after hamstring strain in a digest summary. The case series authors state their findings are most likely not applicable to female players. No non-soccer field sport was studied directly in a late-return setting.

Designs are a case series, a single case, a retrospective association, an observational cohort, an observational team study, a survey, and digest summaries of a cross-sectional study, a meta-analysis, a narrative review and editorials. None tests a structured late-stage week or progress, hold and regress criteria.

Several outcomes are hamstring-specific, and the sprint-exposure data come from healthy squads rather than athletes returning from injury, while the decision context covers any lower-extremity injury.

whatCouldChange.text: Replication of the finding on near-maximal exposure two days before a match in other samples, as the original authors call for, ideally in athletes returning from injury.
Evidence showing whether asymmetry measures taken during late rehabilitation predict outcomes after lower-extremity injury, which would settle their role as progression markers.

evidenceTension.text: One case study proposes step impulse asymmetry to guide phase progression. In collegiate athletes after hamstring strain, strength asymmetry at return to sport did not differ between those who did and did not re-injure, and a narrative review found no evidence that pre-existing asymmetries increase injury risk. On sprint dose, exposure above 95% of maximal speed two days before a match was linked to zero match hamstring injuries in healthy elite squads, though pooled exposure showed no difference, and earlier Gaelic football work cited by another study links weekly exposure to lower injury risk. In a separate soccer cohort, 7 to 8 weekly efforts above 90% were associated with very small eccentric hamstring strength decreases, and injury was not measured. The pack does not resolve how to balance these signals.
